strategy_title: Autotune larger XBLOCK causes register spill and occupancy drop
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (512/1024/2048) caused the compiler to allocate more registers per thread (29→38), which reduced theoretical occupancy from 100% to 75% and achieved occupancy from 75% to 61%. The increased register pressure also caused a 66% increase in executed instructions (2.86M→4.75M), likely due to register spilling or additional index computation at larger tile sizes. Despite eliminating the partial wave, the occupancy loss and instruction count increase more than offset the benefit, resulting in a 39% longer kernel duration (7.26→10.08 µs).
slow_pseudocode:
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):  # XBLOCK=128, 29 regs/thread
    # 100% theoretical occupancy, 75% achieved
    # 2.86M instructions, 7.26 us
applicable_when: Never: this specific pattern caused regression. Avoid when the kernel is already register-pressure-sensitive (registers per thread near the block limit boundary) and theoretical occupancy is at 100%.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel has low register count (≤32/thread) at baseline with 100% theoretical occupancy; increasing XBLOCK will push register count up, reduce block limit from registers, and drop theoretical occupancy below 100%, causing net regression even if partial-wave tail is eliminated. Also avoid when instruction count grows super-linearly with XBLOCK (indicates index recomputation or spill overhead).
framework_notes: In Triton, @triton.autotune with restore_value is required when the kernel writes to an in-out pointer, but the autotune overhead and register pressure from larger XBLOCK configs can negate any launch-configuration benefit. The restore_value=['in_out_ptr0'] addition in the diff is also a correctness concern during autotuning warmup passes.
